entry:
Branch of pure mathematics devoted primarily to the study of the [[Integer|integers]] and arithmetic functions. Number theorists study [[Prime number|prime numbers]], together with objects constructed from integers, such as rational numbers, or defined as generalizations of them, such as algebraic integers. Integers can be considered in themselves or as solutions to equations (Diophantine geometry). Analytic number theory studies objects such as the [[Riemann zeta function]] that encode properties of integers and primes, while Diophantine approximation studies how irrational numbers can be approximated by fractions. Elementary number theory uses elementary methods, and algebraic number theory employs structures such as fields and rings.

The subject is one of the oldest branches of mathematics, alongside geometry. Plimpton 322, a broken clay tablet dated c. 1800 BC, lists Pythagorean triples. Euclid devoted part of his *Elements* to primes and divisibility, giving the [[Euclidean algorithm]] and a proof implying the infinitude of primes. [[Diophantus]] of Alexandria, who probably lived in the 3rd century AD, wrote the *Arithmetica*, a collection of problems seeking rational solutions to polynomial equations.

Number theory deals with statements that are simple to understand but very difficult to solve. [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] was proved 358 years after its original formulation, and Goldbach's conjecture has remained unsolved since the 18th century. [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] remarked, "Mathematics is the queen of the sciences—and number theory is the queen of mathematics." The field was regarded as pure mathematics with no outside applications until the 1970s, when prime numbers became the basis of public-key cryptography algorithms such as the [[RSA cryptosystem]].

Health care profession that integrates the art and science of caring, focusing on the protection, promotion, and optimization of health; the prevention of illness and injury; the facilitation of healing; and the alleviation of suffering. Nurses practice in many specialties with varying levels of certification and responsibility and make up the largest component of most [[Health care|healthcare]] environments. They develop a plan of care in collaboration with physicians, therapists, patients, and families, and they educate the public. Supply and demand for qualified nurses are imbalanced in many countries. In the United Kingdom and the United States, nurse practitioners diagnose health problems and prescribe medications, depending on regulations that vary by state.

In the [[Middle Ages]], nuns and monks often provided nursing-like care in Christian, Islamic, Buddhist, and other traditions. During the [[Reformation]], Protestant reformers closed monasteries and convents, and the profession in Europe was extinguished for approximately 200 years. [[Florence Nightingale]] laid the foundations of professional nursing after the [[Crimean War]], following a statistical study of [[Sanitation|sanitation]] in [[India]]; she reported in 1873 that mortality among soldiers there had declined from 69 to 18 per 1,000 after 10 years of sanitary reform. Her *Notes on Nursing* (1859) was a popular call to action, and her model of nursing education, one of the first connected to a hospital and medical school, spread widely in Europe and North America after 1870. Mary Seacole, who also served in the Crimean War, practiced hygiene and herbal healing. The first nursing school, La Source, was opened in Lausanne, [[Switzerland]], by Valérie de Gasparin and her husband.

Biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life. The intake of these substances provides nutrients, divided into macro- and micronutrients, which are metabolized to create energy and chemical structures; too much or too little of an essential nutrient can cause [[Malnutrition|malnutrition]]. Nutritional science typically emphasizes human nutrition.

The type of organism determines which nutrients it needs and how it obtains them: by consuming organic matter, consuming inorganic matter, absorbing light, or some combination. All forms of life require carbon, energy, and water. Animals require complex nutrients such as [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], [[Lipid|lipids]], and [[Protein|proteins]], obtained by consuming other organisms. Humans developed [[Agriculture|agriculture]] and cooking to replace foraging. Plants acquire nutrients through the soil and atmosphere, and fungi absorb them through the mycelium.

Approximately 30 elements are found in organic matter, with nitrogen, carbon, and phosphorus the most important. Micronutrients, needed in trace amounts, are classified as vitamins (organic) and minerals (inorganic). Essential nutrients are those the body cannot synthesize. Over-nutrition of macronutrients is a major cause of [[Obesity|obesity]] and raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, stroke, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, and some cancers.

Scientific analysis of food began during the chemical revolution of the late 18th century, and modern nutrition science began in the 1910s as micronutrients were identified. Thiamine was the first vitamin chemically identified, in 1926, and in 1932 [[Vitamin C]] was identified as a protection against [[Scurvy|scurvy]]. The first recommended dietary allowances were developed to address fears of deficiency diseases during the Great Depression and the Second World War.

Medical condition, considered a disease by multiple organizations, in which excess body fat has accumulated to such an extent that it can have negative effects on health. People are classified as obese when their [[Body mass index|body mass index]] (BMI), a person's weight divided by the square of height, is over 30 kg/m²; the range 25–30 kg/m² is defined as overweight. Obesity is correlated with [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular diseases]], [[Diabetes|type 2 diabetes]], obstructive sleep apnea, certain types of [[Cancer|cancer]], and [[Osteoarthritis|osteoarthritis]].

Causes include diet, low physical activity, automation, [[Urbanization|urbanization]], genetic susceptibility, medications, mental disorders, economic policies, and endocrine disorders. BMI is criticized because it ignores lean body mass: more than half of NFL players are classified as obese by BMI, yet their mean body fat percentage is 14%, and 40% of college-aged [[Sumo|sumo]] wrestlers in one study were no longer classified as obese when body fat percentage was used.

Diet and exercise are the main recommended treatments, and medications, a gastric balloon, or surgery may be used when they fail. The [[World Health Organization]] stresses that healthy dietary choices should be the most available, affordable, and accessible options. Many people lose weight, but maintaining the loss long-term is rare.

In 2022, over 1 billion people lived with obesity (879 million adults and 159 million children), more than double the adult cases and four times the child cases registered in 1990. The share of adults who were obese rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024, with 18.6% projected by 2030. Obesity is stigmatized in many parts of the world, while some cultures have viewed it as a symbol of wealth and fertility.

Body of salt water covering approximately 70.8% of Earth. The ocean is conventionally divided into five large bodies of water, also called oceans; in descending order by area they are the [[Pacific Ocean]], the [[Atlantic Ocean]], the [[Indian Ocean]], the Antarctic or [[Southern Ocean]], and the [[Arctic Ocean]]. These are mostly divided into seas, gulfs, and smaller bodies of water. The ocean's volume exceeds 1.3 billion cubic km, and its average salinity is roughly 35 grams of dissolved salts per liter. It contains 97% of Earth's water and is the primary component of the [[Hydrosphere|hydrosphere]], acting as a huge reservoir of heat for Earth's energy budget, carbon cycle, and water cycle, and forming the basis for climate and weather patterns worldwide. It harbors most of Earth's animals and protist life, originated [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], and still supplies half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen.

In general use "the ocean" and "the sea" are interchangeable. Strictly, a sea is a body of water, generally a division of the world ocean, partly or fully enclosed by land, such as the North Sea or the Red Sea. The term World Ocean was coined in the early 20th century by the Russian oceanographer Yuly Shokalsky. The word ocean comes from Oceanus, the elder of the Titans in classical Greek mythology, whom the ancient Greeks and Romans believed to be the divine personification of an enormous river encircling the world.

Scientists divide the ocean into horizontal and vertical zones. Horizontally, it covers the oceanic crust and, at its margins, the shallow continental shelves. Vertically, the pelagic zone is the open ocean's water column. The photic zone, defined as the depth at which light intensity is only 1% of the surface value (approximately 200 m in the open ocean), is where photosynthesis occurs and is the most biodiverse zone; the deeper ocean is cold and dark.

Surface temperatures can exceed 30 °C in the tropics and fall to about −2 °C near the poles where sea ice forms; deep ocean temperatures range between −2 °C and 5 °C. Temperature and salinity differences, wind, tides, and the Coriolis effect drive currents such as the [[Gulf Stream]], Kuroshio Current, Agulhas Current, and Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which transport water, gases, pollutants, and heat around the world. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it undergoes acidification, a drop in pH.

Geological evidence from the Isua Greenstone Belt shows that water existed on Earth 3.8 billion years ago, though the origin of Earth's oceans is unknown. The ocean is the habitat of over 230,000 known species, perhaps over two million in all. It provides ecosystem services, seafood, and transport, but faces marine pollution, overfishing, warming, acidification, and sea level rise.

Geographical region in the Pacific Ocean including [[Australasia]], [[Melanesia]], [[Micronesia]], and [[Polynesia]]. Outside the English-speaking world, Oceania is generally considered a continent, with mainland Australia as its continental landmass. Spanning the Eastern and Western hemispheres, it has a land area of about 9,000,000 sq km and a population of around 44.4 million as of 2022, making it the smallest continent in land area and the second-least populated after Antarctica. [[Australia]] is its largest and most populous country and Sydney its largest city. Puncak Jaya in Indonesia, at 4,884 m, is the highest peak.

Economies range from the highly developed markets of Australia, French Polynesia, Hawaii, New Caledonia, and New Zealand, which rank high in the Human Development Index, to the much less developed economies of Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, and Western New Guinea. Most countries are parliamentary democracies, and tourism is a large source of income for the Pacific island nations.

The first settlers of Australia, New Guinea, and the large islands just to the east arrived more than 60,000 years ago. The rock art of [[Aboriginal Australians]] is the longest continuously practiced artistic tradition in the world. Europeans first explored the region from the 16th century onward: between 1512 and 1526 Portuguese explorers reached the Tanimbar Islands, some of the Caroline Islands, and west New Guinea, followed by Spanish, Dutch, British, and French explorers. On his first voyage, [[James Cook]] went to Tahiti and followed the east coast of Australia for the first time; he later reached the Hawaiian Islands. Britain established a penal colony in Australia in 1788. European settlement significantly altered the social and political landscape, and the Pacific theater saw major action in both world wars.

The name derives from the French *Océanie*, from the Greek word for ocean, and was coined by French geographers in the early 19th century; it reflects the ocean's role in linking the region's parts. Definitions vary. The broadest encompasses the islands between mainland Asia and the Americas, with Zealandia usually considered a microcontinent. The United Nations has used a definition since 1947 based on four subregions, Australasia, Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia, which excludes Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Singapore, and Taiwan. In 1973 anthropologists Roger Green and Andrew Pawley proposed the terms Near Oceania and Remote Oceania. The islands generally considered the geographic extremes are the Bonin Islands (Japan), Hawaii (United States), Clipperton Island (France), Easter Island (Chile), and Macquarie Island (Australia).

Range of ages for people nearing and surpassing [[Life expectancy|life expectancy]]. Old people are also called the elderly, elders, senior citizens, seniors, or older adults. Old age is not a definite biological stage: the chronological age denoted as old varies culturally and historically. Disciplines concerned with it include the study of the organic processes of [[Ageing|aging]] (senescence), gerontology, [[Geriatrics|geriatrics]], and gerontechnology.

There is no universal official definition. Most developed Western countries set the [[Retirement|retirement]] age around 65, generally taken to mark the transition from middle to old age. The [[United Nations]] considers old age to begin at 60, while a 2001 joint report by the U.S. National Institute on Aging and the World Health Organization's Regional Office for Africa set it at 50 in Sub-Saharan Africa, where old age is determined by a person's ability to contribute to society and life expectancy is lower.

Gerontologists recognize diversity within old age. In developed countries many people in their later 60s and 70s remain fit and active, while after age 80 they generally become increasingly frail; some, called "superagers," retain vitality much longer. One study distinguishes the young-old (60 to 69), the middle-old (70 to 79), and the very old (80+). Scholars list chronological, biological, psychological, and social dimensions of old age, to which Wattis and Curran add a developmental one.

Older people often have limited regenerative abilities and are more susceptible to illness and injury. They face social problems related to retirement, [[Loneliness|loneliness]], and ageism: a 2023 U.S. poll found that about 37% of adults aged 50 to 80 experienced loneliness. In 2011 the United Nations proposed a human-rights convention to protect old people.

Branch of philosophy that studies being, traditionally understood as the subdiscipline of [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]] concerned with the most general features of reality. Ontology examines the characteristics shared by all things and their classification into basic types, such as particulars and universals. Particulars are unique, non-repeatable entities, such as [[Socrates]], whereas universals are general, repeatable entities, such as the color green. Concrete objects exist in space and time; abstract objects, such as the number 5, exist outside them. Systems of categories employ notions such as substance, property, relation, state of affairs, and event.

Ontologists disagree about which entities exist at the most basic level. Platonic realism holds that universals exist objectively, conceptualism that they exist only in the mind, and nominalism denies their existence. [[Materialism]] posits that fundamentally only matter exists, whereas dualism holds that mind and matter are independent principles. [[George Berkeley]] proposed that all existence is mental, in the slogan "to be is to be perceived." Methods include the analysis of concepts and experience, the use of intuitions and [[Thought experiment|thought experiments]], and the integration of findings from natural science.

Formal ontology investigates the most abstract features of objects, while applied ontology studies entities in specific domains; social ontology, for example, examines basic concepts of the social sciences. In information and computer science, an ontology is a formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualization of a domain, a usage popularized in the 1990s, and it allows the structured storage of information in a [[Database|database]].

The relation between ontology and metaphysics is disputed, and some philosophers use the terms as synonyms. The ancient Greeks did not use the word, which was coined by philosophers in the 17th century.

Branch of physics that studies the behavior, manipulation, and detection of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]], including its interactions with matter and with instruments that use or detect it. Optics usually describes visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light, and extends to radio waves, microwaves, and X-rays.

Geometric optics treats light as rays that travel in straight lines and bend when they pass through or reflect from surfaces. Physical optics adds wave effects such as [[Diffraction|diffraction]] and interference. The ray model was developed first, followed by the wave model; 19th-century progress in electromagnetic theory, notably by [[James Clerk Maxwell]], showed that light waves are electromagnetic radiation. Phenomena that depend on light's wave-like and particle-like properties require quantum mechanics, which models light as particles called [[Photon|photons]]. Optics is relevant to astronomy, engineering, photography, and medicine, and underlies mirrors, lenses, telescopes, microscopes, lasers, and fiber optics.

The earliest known lenses, of polished crystal, date from as early as 2000 BC from Crete. Greek philosophers split between the intromission theory of vision, held by Democritus, Epicurus, and Aristotle, and the emission theory articulated by Plato. [[Euclid]] linked vision to geometry in a treatise on optics. In 984 the Persian mathematician Ibn Sahl described a law of refraction equivalent to [[Snell's law]]. In the early 11th century [[Ibn al-Haytham]] wrote the *Book of Optics*, rejecting emission theories and proposing that light reflects in straight lines from every point of a viewed object into the eye. In the 17th century Isaac Newton proposed a particle model of light and [[Christiaan Huygens]] a wave explanation. Lasers were developed in 1960.

Form of human communication in which knowledge, art, beliefs, ideas, and culture are received, preserved, and transmitted orally from one generation to the next. Transmission is through speech or song and may include folktales, ballads, chants, prose, or poetry. The information is held by oral repositories, sometimes called "walking libraries," who are usually also performers, such as griots in West Africa. Societies use oral tradition to pass on oral history, oral literature, oral law, and other knowledge, either without a writing system or alongside one. It is the most widespread medium of human communication.

[[Folklore]] is one type of oral tradition. [[Buddhism]], [[Hinduism]], Catholicism, Yazidism, and [[Jainism]] have used it, in parallel to writing, to transmit canonical scriptures, rituals, hymns, and mythologies. The scholar John Foley calls it "the single most dominant communicative technology of our species."

African societies have broadly been labeled oral civilizations. In Africa the principal political, legal, social, and religious texts were transmitted orally, and when the Bamums in [[Cameroon]] invented a script, the first texts written down were the royal chronicle and the code of customary law. Most African courts had archivists who learned the royal genealogy by heart. Performance context shapes content: in Burundi traditions were short because they were told at informal gatherings where everyone took a turn, whereas in neighboring [[Rwanda]] a professional performer had to entertain a patron for a whole evening.

The fidelity of oral traditions varies. The Kyrgyz *Manas* cycle, exceeding 500,000 lines, has been recited across generations, yet traditions remain susceptible to telescoped timelines and conflations, so they serve as historical sources most reliably when corroborated by independent evidence.
